A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AMSE loss and GraphCast fine-tuning study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original GraphCast fine-tuning results, including spectral resolution, lagged-ensemble verification, tropical-cyclone prediction and comparisons with station observations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds MSE/MAE fine-tuning comparisons, filtered forecast visualizations and a finite-ensemble bias analysis.

M1.justification: The proposed AMSE loss in Equation (6), variable/level weighting, GraphCast architecture and forecasting procedure are retained. The added MSE and MAE variants are comparison controls, rather than changes to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same HRES/ERA5 training coverage, 2022 weather evaluation, tropical-cyclone observations and North American station comparisons. The added controls reuse existing forecasting tasks, and the new filtered visualization examines the existing winter storm Eunice case.

E2.justification: Appendix B.5, Figure 14 and Table 2 add MSE AR12 and MAE AR12 as evaluated comparators. MSE AR12 is distinct from the retained, unmodified Control: it receives the fine-tuning curriculum, providing an important additional-training control. MAE AR12 adds a competing loss-function comparison.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the reported warm-up from 128 to 64 batches per stage. Appendix B.4 revises SER to form spatially aggregated variance/error ratios; B.4.1 adds bias-adjusted ensemble-error evaluation. The new visualization uses a fourth-order high-pass filter with cutoff wavenumber 50, while the new loss controls reuse the existing curriculum. These are localized protocol additions and revisions; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained AR1/AR12 and spectral analyses, v2 adds matched-curriculum loss ablations testing whether extra training explains improved sharpness (B.5), a high-pass analysis of Eunice forecast structures (B.1), and an analysis of finite-ensemble error bias (B.4.1). The new training control addresses a central attribution question absent from v1.

E5.justification: v2 adds finite-ensemble bias estimation and a variance-subtraction correction for ensemble mean squared error, and explicitly uses unbiased ensemble variance in SER. The existing one-third-date bootstrap sampling and 90% significance threshold remain. No additional training seeds or repeated-run counts are reported.

E6.justification: New results establish that MSE/MAE fine-tuning retains fine-scale smoothing, although MAE improves intermediate-scale sharpness. Table 2 adds substantive comparisons: five-day z500 CRPS is 82.100 for MSE AR12, 80.621 for MAE AR12 and 80.469 for AMSE AR12; five-day q700 instead favors MAE, 0.499 versus AMSE's 0.510. Figure 13 adds results under the bias-adjusted metric, and some significance markers change in retained scorecards. The headline resolution and cyclone findings remain.

T1.justification: Appendix B.4.1 adds a derivation of the finite-ensemble squared-error bias, including the variance divided by ensemble-size term, and defines its correction in Equation (18). The SER definition also changes its normalization and spatial aggregation. The central AMSE derivation and Appendix A's KL-divergence analysis are unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements retain the same central claims: a parameter-free loss modification produces sharper deterministic forecasts, improves effective resolution from 1,250 km to 160 km, and benefits ensemble spread, cyclone intensity and wind extremes. The added evidence supports these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds focused qualifications about the meaning of effective resolution, the untested use of AMSE throughout training, and possible regularization benefits of MSE. It also explains why multiscale separation is necessary to prevent coarse-scale variance from concealing missing fine-scale variability. Existing precipitation, lagged-ensemble and out-of-distribution limitations remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises training-code release upon publication. v2 instead reports access locations and licenses for the AMSE implementation, training code and fine-tuned checkpoints. It also documents the new loss-control configurations and filtering parameters. This substantially expands actionable reproducibility information, although external resource availability was not independently checked.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant antecedents and approaches, including Weyn, Keisler, Allen, Han and Lippe, and relates AMSE to Chakraborty's binned spectral power loss. Kent and Leutbecher–Palmer support the new resolution discussion and bias analysis. The central positioning relative to ensemble methods and NeuralGCM remains; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. Local changes expand the introduction and discussion, number the This Work subsection, rename Discussion as Discussion & Limitations, add appendix subsections, and update author, affiliation and acknowledgement text.

P2.justification: The main text and references are comprehensively reformatted from a single-column preprint into a two-column conference layout, with figures resized and relocated. v2 adds Figures 7, 13 and 14 and Table 2, adds a length-scale axis to the effective-resolution plot, and revises labels and captions in retained plots. These are substantial visual changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: v1 compares AMSE fine-tuning principally with an untouched checkpoint, leaving extra training as a confound, and only promises future code. v2's matched-curriculum MSE/MAE controls directly address that attribution gap, while its code/checkpoint access information substantially improves reproducibility documentation. The finite-ensemble analysis and clearer resolution qualifications further strengthen evaluation. A local mean/median inconsistency in the new MAE explanation does not outweigh these substantive gains.
